chunks: 12 volts across a 1 ohm coil: 12 amps?.
The question: If I hook up a 12 volts supply (with infinite current output) to a motor/solenoid with a coil resistance of 1 ohm, will I see 12 amps of curent being draw? Why?
When would I see 12 amps? When wouldn't I?
Ohm's law says 12 volts across 1 ohms gives 12 amps. That number is real, but it is only where the current ends up, not where it starts.
A coil also has inductance, so the current ramps up gradually. And if the coil belongs to a spinning motor, the motor's own back-EMF keeps the current well below 12 amps.
Think of water in a long, heavy pipe when you open the tap. The water has to get moving first, so the flow builds up gradually.
The pipe's friction sets the final flow, but the water's heaviness sets how fast it gets there.
In a coil, resistance sets the final 12 amps and inductance sets how fast the current climbs.
The analogy breaks for a motor: a spinning motor lowers the limit itself, as if a pump at the far end pushed back.
The naive answer (dashed) jumps to 12 amps. The real current takes about five time constants (25 milliseconds here) to get there.
A bigger solenoid with L equals 100 millihenries would take half a second.
Drag L up to 100 millihenries and 5τ moves out to half a second; the time axis follows τ, so the curve keeps its shape while the tick labels stretch twentyfold.
Drag R up and both the time constant and the final current fall.
Ohm's law: I equals V over R . The current through a resistor is voltage divided by resistance.
Inductance (L): how strongly a coil resists changes in its current, measured in henries (1 millihenries is a thousandth of a henry).
Time constant ( tau equals L over R ): how long the current takes to rise about 63% of the way to its final value. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor makes against the supply.
Stall: shaft held still, so there is no back-EMF.
Put 12 volts across a 1 ohms coil with 5 millihenries of inductance. The time constant is 5 millihenries / 1 ohms = 5 milliseconds.
After 5 milliseconds the current is about 63% of 12 amps, roughly 7. 6 amps. If this coil is a motor that spins up and builds 11.
5 volts of back-EMF, the current falls to (12 minus 11. 5) / 1 = 0. 5 amps.
That is the whole idea: 12 amps is a limit, reached over time, and only for a solenoid or a stalled motor.
"Not instantly, and for a motor usually not at all. Twelve amps is V over R, the limit.
The coil is an inductor, so the current rises as 12 times one minus e to the minus t over tau, with tau equal to L over R.
A DC solenoid reaches 12 amps in steady state after about five time constants, and that's 144 watts, so it will burn out.
A motor draws 12 amps only at stall: spinning, back-EMF cuts it to maybe half an amp. In AC, with a hot coil, or with extra wiring resistance, it would be lower."
